claim: Microglia are the brain's resident immune cells with a tremendous capacity to autonomously self-renew.
source: Microglia are the brain's resident immune cells with a tremendous capacity to autonomously self-renew.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that characterizes microglia based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Cortical microglia show limited turnover and migration under basal conditions.
source: Using chronic in vivo two-photon imaging in awake mice, we confirm that cortical microglia show limited turnover and migration under basal conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Following depletion, microglial repopulation is remarkably rapid and is sustained by the dynamic division of remaining microglia.
source: Following depletion, however, microglial repopulation is remarkably rapid and is sustained by the dynamic division of remaining microglia, in a manner that is largely independent of signaling through the P2Y12 receptor.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations from in vivo imaging during repopulation.

claim: Microglial repopulation is largely independent of signaling through the P2Y12 receptor.
source: Following depletion, however, microglial repopulation is remarkably rapid and is sustained by the dynamic division of remaining microglia, in a manner that is largely independent of signaling through the P2Y12 receptor.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of repopulation dynamics in wild-type and P2Y12 knockout mice.

claim: Mathematical modeling of microglial division demonstrates that the observed division rates can account for the rapid repopulation observed in vivo.
source: Mathematical modeling of microglial division demonstrates that the observed division rates can account for the rapid repopulation observed in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling based on empirical division rate data.

claim: Newly born microglia resemble mature microglia within days of repopulation.
source: Additionally, newly born microglia resemble mature microglia within days of repopulation, although morphological maturation is different in newly born microglia in P2Y12 knock out mice.
evidence: This is supported by morphological and functional analyses of newly born microglia.

claim: Morphological maturation is different in newly born microglia in P2Y12 knock out mice.
source: Additionally, newly born microglia resemble mature microglia within days of repopulation, although morphological maturation is different in newly born microglia in P2Y12 knock out mice.
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis comparing wild-type and P2Y12 KO mice.

claim: Newly born microglia do not recapitulate the slow maturation seen in development but instead take on mature roles in the CNS.
source: Our work suggests that microglia rapidly locally and that newly born microglia do not recapitulate the slow maturation seen in development but instead take on mature roles in the CNS.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the rapid acquisition of mature characteristics by newly born microglia.

claim: Microglia are the brain's resident tissue macrophages.
source: Microglia are the brain's resident tissue macrophages (Crotti et al., 2016; Ginhoux et al., 2010) with a developmental origin that is distinct from other macrophages (Ginhoux et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Microglia have a developmental origin that is distinct from other macrophages.
source: Microglia are the brain's resident tissue macrophages (Crotti et al., 2016; Ginhoux et al., 2010) with a developmental origin that is distinct from other macrophages (Ginhoux et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: In mice, microglial progenitor cells derive from the yolk sac and populate the brain before the blood-brain barrier forms.
source: In mice, microglial progenitor cells derive from the yolk sac and populate the brain before the blood-brain barrier forms (Ginhoux et al., 2010; Kierdorf et al., 2013) slowly acquiring mature gene expression over two to three weeks (Bennett et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Microglial progenitor cells slowly acquire mature gene expression over two to three weeks.
source: In mice, microglial progenitor cells derive from the yolk sac and populate the brain before the blood-brain barrier forms (Ginhoux et al., 2010; Kierdorf et al., 2013) slowly acquiring mature gene expression over two to three weeks (Bennett et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: In both the rodent and human brain, microglial numbers are maintained throughout adult life.
source: In both the rodent and human brain, microglial numbers are maintained throughout adult life (Réu et al., 2017; Füger et al., 2017; Hashimoto et al., 2013), with no further contribution of peripheral macrophages to the microglial population in the absence of pathological changes (Ajami et al., 2007; Askew et al., 2017; Bruttger et al., 2015; Elmore et al., 2015; Mildner et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: There is no further contribution of peripheral macrophages to the microglial population in the absence of pathological changes.
source: In both the rodent and human brain, microglial numbers are maintained throughout adult life (Réu et al., 2017; Füger et al., 2017; Hashimoto et al., 2013), with no further contribution of peripheral macrophages to the microglial population in the absence of pathological changes (Ajami et al., 2007; Askew et al., 2017; Bruttger et al., 2015; Elmore et al., 2015; Mildner et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Microglia are uniformly distributed in a distinct cellular grid throughout the brain parenchyma.
source: Microglia are uniformly distributed in a distinct cellular grid throughout the brain parenchyma (Nimmerjahn et al., 2005; Eyo et al., 2018; Hefendehl et al., 2014) and maintain their territories with slow translocation on a timescale of days (Eyo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Microglia maintain their territories with slow translocation on a timescale of days.
source: Microglia are uniformly distributed in a distinct cellular grid throughout the brain parenchyma (Nimmerjahn et al., 2005; Eyo et al., 2018; Hefendehl et al., 2014) and maintain their territories with slow translocation on a timescale of days (Eyo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Microglia are long-lived cells.
source: Although microglia are long-lived cells, they do self-renew slowly under physiological conditions (Füger et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Microglia self-renew slowly under physiological conditions.
source: Although microglia are long-lived cells, they do self-renew slowly under physiological conditions (Füger et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Recent studies have pharmacologically and genetically depleted microglia and uncovered a remarkable capacity for rapid repopulation of the microglial niche without a contribution of infiltrating monocytes.
source: To study microglial self-renewal, recent studies have pharmacologically and genetically depleted microglia and uncovered a remarkable capacity for rapid repopulation of the microglial niche without a contribution of infiltrating monocytes (Ajami et al., 2007; Elmore et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Early studies in fixed sections from mice following depletion suggested that microglia rapidly repopulate, possibly through a microglial progenitor population which can divide in large proliferative macroclusters from which newly born microglia migrate throughout the brain.
source: Early studies in fixed sections from mice following depletion suggested that microglia rapidly repopulate, possibly through a microglial progenitor population which can divide in large proliferative macroclusters from which newly born microglia migrate throughout the brain (Bruttger et al., 2015; Elmore et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: More recent studies have shown that surviving microglia divide and transiently express nestin; however, none of the repopulated microglia derive from nestin progenitors.
source: More recent studies have shown that surviving microglia divide and transiently express nestin; however, none of the repopulated microglia derive from nestin progenitors (Huang et al., 2018a; Huang et al., 2018b; Zhan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Microglial repopulation in the retina is driven by remaining microglia; however, proliferation occurs in the central retina, suggesting a specific site of microglial generation in the eye.
source: Similar to repopulation in the cortex, microglial repopulation in the retina is driven by remaining microglia; however, proliferation occurs in the central retina, suggesting a specific site of microglial generation in the eye (Huang et al., 2018b; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In the retina, repopulated microglia eventually adopted the dynamic features of endogenous microglia before depletion.
source: In the retina, repopulated microglia eventually adopted the dynamic features of endogenous microglia before depletion (Zhang et al., 2018), and repopulated cortical microglia also have expression patterns similar to those of endogenous microglia 30 days after repopulation (Bruttger et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2018b; Zhan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Repopulated cortical microglia have expression patterns similar to those of endogenous microglia 30 days after repopulation.
source: In the retina, repopulated microglia eventually adopted the dynamic features of endogenous microglia before depletion (Zhang et al., 2018), and repopulated cortical microglia also have expression patterns similar to those of endogenous microglia 30 days after repopulation (Bruttger et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2018b; Zhan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Genomic analysis of newly born cortical microglia shows that new microglia within days of repopulation recapitulate developmental expression profiles.
source: Genomic analysis of newly born cortical microglia shows that new microglia within days of repopulation recapitulate developmental expression profiles (Elmore et al., 2015; Zhan et al., 2019), suggesting that they may undergo a stepwise maturation after repopulation that resembles developmental maturation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: New microglia may undergo a stepwise maturation after repopulation that resembles developmental maturation.
source: Genomic analysis of newly born cortical microglia shows that new microglia within days of repopulation recapitulate developmental expression profiles (Elmore et al., 2015; Zhan et al., 2019), suggesting that they may undergo a stepwise maturation after repopulation that resembles developmental maturation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on cited genomic analysis.

claim: Microglial self-renewal is slow under basal conditions, with microglia maintaining their territories and showing little movement, loss, or proliferation.
source: We show that microglial self-renewal is slow under basal conditions, with microglia maintaining their territories and showing little movement, loss, or proliferation.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Following depletion, newly born microglia rapidly repopulate the brain and acquire equal cell-to-cell spacing reminiscent of baseline conditions.
source: In agreement with previous studies, we show that, following depletion, newly born microglia rapidly repopulate the brain and acquire equal cell-to-cell spacing reminiscent of baseline conditions.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo imaging data and nearest neighbor analysis.

claim: Self-renewal is driven locally by residual microglia, which have a capacity for fast and continued self-division.
source: Self-renewal is driven locally by residual microglia, which have a capacity for fast and continued self-division.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo imaging showing division of residual microglia.

claim: The observed division rates could account for the rapid repopulation.
source: To determine whether other mechanisms such as migration from sites outside of the imaging area contributed to the increase in microglia numbers, we mathematically modeled microglial self-renewal in vivo and showed that the observed division rates could account for the rapid repopulation.
evidence: This is supported by mathematical modeling based on empirical division rates.

claim: Newly born microglia quickly acquire ramified morphologies and dynamic surveillance capabilities in response to focal injury.
source: Finally, we showed that newly born microglia quickly acquire ramified morphologies and dynamic surveillance capabilities in response to focal injury, suggesting that microglial functional maturation is remarkably rapid in the adult brain and does not recapitulate developmental features.
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis and laser ablation experiments.

claim: Microglial functional maturation is remarkably rapid in the adult brain and does not recapitulate developmental features.
source: Finally, we showed that newly born microglia quickly acquire ramified morphologies and dynamic surveillance capabilities in response to focal injury, suggesting that microglial functional maturation is remarkably rapid in the adult brain and does not recapitulate developmental features.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the rapid acquisition of mature characteristics.

claim: P2Y12 is highly expressed exclusively in microglia in the brain.
source: P2Y12 is highly expressed exclusively in microglia in the brain (Bennett et al., 2016) and regulates microglial translocation under physiological conditions in vivo (Haynes et al., 2006; Eyo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: P2Y12 regulates microglial translocation under physiological conditions in vivo.
source: P2Y12 is highly expressed exclusively in microglia in the brain (Bennett et al., 2016) and regulates microglial translocation under physiological conditions in vivo (Haynes et al., 2006; Eyo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Neither microglial repopulation nor the maturation of newly-born microglia was altered by P2Y12 loss.
source: Neither microglial repopulation nor the maturation of newly-born microglia was altered by P2Y12 loss.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of wild-type and P2Y12 knockout mice.

claim: The microglia landscape following depletion is restored through a rapid division of remaining microglia, local migration to fill the microglia niche, and fast acquisition of mature characteristics soon after repopulation without the need for P2Y12 signaling.
source: These findings suggest that the microglia landscape following depletion is restored through a rapid division of remaining microglia, local migration to fill the microglia niche, and fast acquisition of mature characteristics soon after repopulation without the need for P2Y12 signaling.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Microglia in the same cortical area could easily be imaged and tracked from day to day without overt changes in microglial morphology.
source: Microglia in the same cortical area could easily be imaged and tracked from day to day (Figure 1A and Video 1) without overt changes in microglial morphology, which could indicate immune activation over time.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo imaging data shown in Figure 1A and Video 1.

claim: Microglia numbers were stable over 14 consecutive days.
source: Microglia numbers were stable over 14 consecutive days, and individual microglia could be re-identified in the same location daily over this period, suggesting limited local migration and maintenance of microglial territories during this time (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo imaging data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Individual microglia could be re-identified in the same location daily over 14 days, suggesting limited local migration and maintenance of microglial territories during this time.
source: Microglia numbers were stable over 14 consecutive days, and individual microglia could be re-identified in the same location daily over this period, suggesting limited local migration and maintenance of microglial territories during this time (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo imaging data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Microglia generally maintain their territories, whereby each microglia soma lies at ~30 μm from its nearest neighboring microglia.
source: Quantitative three-dimensional nearest neighbor (NN) analysis revealed that microglia generally maintain their territories, whereby each microglia soma lies at ~30 μm from its nearest neighboring microglia.
evidence: This is supported by nearest neighbor analysis of imaging data.

claim: The nearest neighbor distance remained similar on subsequent days and between animals.
source: This NN distance remained similar on subsequent days and between animals (Figure 1B, n=3, 16–17 microglia per mouse, 30–40 μm stacks).
evidence: This is supported by nearest neighbor analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: On average, microglia shifted on the order of 15 μm from day to day.
source: On average, microglia shifted on the order of 15 μm from day to day (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by translocation index analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The translocation index increased as the two imaging sessions were further apart in time.
source: This number increased as the two imaging sessions were further apart in time (Figure 1D), possibly due to tissue distortion over time.
evidence: This is supported by translocation index analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Most microglia did not move by more than 10 μm in either short or long comparisons.
source: In general, most microglia did not move by more than 10 μm in either short (1–2 day), (1–4 day), (1–7 day) and long (1–10 day), (1–12 day), (1–14 day) comparisons.
evidence: This is supported by translocation analysis.

claim: The proportion of microglia that moved more than 30 μm was small in both short and long-term comparisons.
source: The proportion of microglia that moved more than 30 μm (the territory of single microglia) was small in both short and long-term comparisons (Figure 1D–E, n=3, 16–17 microglia per mouse, 30–40 μm stacks).
evidence: This is supported by translocation analysis shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: Microglia are stable under basal conditions and show limited movement within their territory over 14 days.
source: Overall, this analysis suggests that microglia are stable under basal conditions and show limited movement within their territory over 14 days.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the translocation and nearest neighbor data.

claim: With the introduction of PLX for 7 days, microglia numbers in the visual cortex decreased by 75%.
source: With the introduction of PLX for 7 days, microglia numbers in the visual cortex decreased by 75% (Figure 2A,B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and the 3D NN number increased to 200 μm reflecting the decreased density and therefore increased distance between remaining microglia (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of microglia numbers shown in Figure 2A,B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The 3D nearest neighbor number increased to 200 μm reflecting the decreased density and therefore increased distance between remaining microglia after PLX treatment.
source: With the introduction of PLX for 7 days, microglia numbers in the visual cortex decreased by 75% (Figure 2A,B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and the 3D NN number increased to 200 μm reflecting the decreased density and therefore increased distance between remaining microglia (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by nearest neighbor analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: No changes in cytokine production or astrocyte morphology were observed following depletion.
source: We did not observe changes in cytokine production or astrocyte morphology following depletion (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by cytokine assays and GFAP immunostaining shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Newly born microglia rapidly repopulated the visual cortex, and microglia numbers were almost completely restored after only 3 days of repopulation.
source: Newly born microglia rapidly repopulated the visual cortex, and microglia numbers were almost completely restored after only 3 days of repopulation.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo imaging data tracking microglial numbers during repopulation.

claim: The newly generated microglia surpassed baseline numbers after 5–7 days of repopulation.
source: In addition, the newly generated microglia surpassed baseline numbers after 5–7 days of repopulation (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of microglial numbers shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The 3D nearest neighbor distance returned to control levels after 3 days of repopulation and remained relatively stable until 30 days of repopulation.
source: In concert, the 3D NN distance returned to control levels after 3 days of repopulation and remained relatively stable until 30 days of repopulation, the last time point examined, at which time the number of microglia was similar to that of control microglia numbers before PLX treatment (Figure 2C and Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by nearest neighbor analysis shown in Figure 2C and Video 2.

claim: Microglial proliferation occurs very rapidly over a 24-hr period starting at ~2 days after cessation of PLX treatment.
source: These results suggest that microglial proliferation occurs very rapidly over a 24-hr period starting at ~2 days after cessation of PLX treatment and that microglia rapidly regain their territories within the visual cortex, maintaining their equal spacing and numbers after repopulation is complete.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the repopulation kinetics data.

claim: Microglia rapidly regain their territories within the visual cortex, maintaining their equal spacing and numbers after repopulation is complete.
source: These results suggest that microglial proliferation occurs very rapidly over a 24-hr period starting at ~2 days after cessation of PLX treatment and that microglia rapidly regain their territories within the visual cortex, maintaining their equal spacing and numbers after repopulation is complete.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the repopulation and nearest neighbor data.

claim: PLX treatment in P2Y12-KO mice caused a depletion of microglia of ~70%.
source: PLX treatment in P2Y12-KO/CX3CR1-GFP (which will be abbreviated to P2Y12-KO henceforth) mice caused a depletion of microglia of ~70% (Figure 2D), with a concomitant increase in 3D NN (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of microglial numbers in P2Y12-KO mice shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The change in nearest neighbor distance was not as profound in P2Y12-KO mice as in CX3CR1-GFP mice, possibly because these animals had, on average, smaller magnitudes of depletion.
source: The change in NN distance was not as profound as in CX3CR1-GFP mice, possibly because these animals had, on average, smaller magnitudes of depletion, although depletion was highly variable across all animals examined irrespective of genotype (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the nearest neighbor data comparing genotypes, shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Microglia repopulated in a temporal pattern similar to CX3CR1-GFP mice after cessation of the inhibitor in P2Y12-KO mice.
source: While microglia repopulated in a temporal pattern similar to CX3CR1-GFP mice after cessation of the inhibitor (Figure 2D,E), there appeared to be a slight delay in early repopulation (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of repopulation kinetics shown in Figure 2D,E,G.

claim: There appeared to be a slight delay in early repopulation in P2Y12-KO mice.
source: While microglia repopulated in a temporal pattern similar to CX3CR1-GFP mice after cessation of the inhibitor (Figure 2D,E), there appeared to be a slight delay in early repopulation (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of repopulation kinetics shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The delay in early repopulation in P2Y12-KO mice resolved quickly, and on day 5 and beyond, microglial repopulation matched CX3CR1-GFP controls.
source: However, this delay resolved quickly, and on day 5 and beyond, microglial repopulation matched CX3CR1-GFP controls (Figure 2H,I and Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of repopulation kinetics shown in Figure 2H,I and supplementary figures.

claim: P2Y12 signaling plays a minor role in repopulation dynamics.
source: This suggests that P2Y12 signaling plays a minor role in repopulation dynamics.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the similar repopulation kinetics in wild-type and P2Y12-KO mice.

claim: During the repopulation phase, occasional splitting of existing microglia into two daughter cells was observed.
source: During the repopulation phase, we observed occasional splitting of existing microglia into two daughter cells (Figure 3), which has been reported previously (Füger et al., 2017; Tay et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo imaging data shown in Figure 3 and citations to previous research.

claim: Both new cells from microglial division were present in subsequent imaging sessions, indicating that these cells persist and become integrated with the microglial network.
source: Both new cells were present in subsequent imaging sessions, indicating that these cells persist and become integrated with the microglial network (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Doublet microglia during repopulation had larger and more elongated somas than either control microglia or singlet microglia during repopulation.
source: Doublet microglia during repopulation, had larger and more elongated somas than either control microglia or singlet microglia during repopulation although all these parameters overlapped in the three microglia populations (Figure 3I–K).
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis shown in Figure 3I-K.

claim: A combination of soma perimeter and soma elongation effectively separated out doublet microglia from singlet microglia after repopulation and from microglia in control animals.
source: A combination of soma perimeter and soma elongation effectively separated out doublet microglia from singlet microglia after repopulation and from microglia in control animals, showing that doublet microglia have a distinct morphological signature.
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis.

claim: Singlet microglia show a larger morphological diversity than control microglia, suggesting that newly born microglia themselves may have an altered morphology.
source: It is notable that this analysis suggests that singlet microglia show a larger morphological diversity than control microglia, suggesting that newly born microglia themselves may have an altered morphology.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the morphological analysis data.

claim: Galectin-3 expression was increased in repopulating microglia, although its expression was not statistically significantly different between doublet and singlet microglia.
source: Interestingly, Galectin-3 expression was increased in repopulating microglia, although its expression was not statistically significantly different between doublet and singlet microglia (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), recapitulating previous results showing that proliferating microglia can be Galectin-3 positive or negative (Zhan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by Galectin-3 immunostaining shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and citation to previous research.

claim: Only a subset of doublet cells was Galectin-3 positive.
source: Additionally, only a subset of doublet cells was Galectin-3 positive.
evidence: This is supported by Galectin-3 immunostaining data.

claim: The number of doublet cells per field increased around day 3 to day 5 of repopulation.
source: We quantified both the total number of doublets and the percentage of all microglia that were doublets during our imaging of depletion and repopulation and found that both these measures were increased in the repopulation phase (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of doublet cells shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: Similar dynamics of doublet microglia was observed in P2Y12-KO, suggesting that P2Y12 signaling did not play a large role in regulating microglial division.
source: Similar dynamics of doublet microglia was observed in P2Y12-KO, again suggesting that P2Y12 signaling did not play a large role in regulating microglial division (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of doublet dynamics in wild-type and P2Y12-KO mice shown in Figure 3D,E.

claim: The time scale of the division of each doublet was slow, with microglia remaining in the doublet state for days before dividing.
source: Second, the time scale of the division of each doublet was slow, with microglia remaining in the doublet state for days before dividing, making it unlikely that these cells could create the large increases seen in microglial numbers within 3 days (Figures 2B and 3B,C).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the imaging data showing doublet persistence.

claim: The percentage of microglia that were in a doublet state was low even during peak repopulation, and this level of doublets in the microglial population was maintained long after microglial repopulation was complete.
source: Third, the percentage of microglia that were in a doublet state was low even during peak repopulation, and this level of doublets in the microglial population was maintained long after microglial repopulation was complete (Figures 2B and 3B,C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of doublet percentages shown in Figures 2B and 3B,C.

claim: A microglial division could be remarkably rapid where doublets separated into two daughter cells in as little as 4 hr.
source: Unlike what we observed during once per day imaging sessions (Figure 2 and Figure 3), a microglial division could be remarkably rapid where doublets separated into two daughter cells in as little as 4 hr (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by high-frequency imaging data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: 91% of new cells were associated with a characteristic increase and elongation of the cell soma of the original cell before it divided into two microglia.
source: In an analysis of a subset of divisions where cells could be clearly tracked throughout the 24-hr period (22 total from three animals), we found that 91% of new cells were associated with a characteristic increase and elongation of the cell soma of the original cell before it divided into two microglia.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of division events during high-frequency imaging.

claim: Original microglia often had extensive processes, which were maintained during the division and generation of new microglia (95%).
source: Original microglia often had extensive processes, which were maintained during the division and generation of new microglia (95%), and newly generated microglia frequently had a ramified microglia arbor on the same day that division was complete (82%).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of division events during high-frequency imaging.

claim: Newly generated microglia frequently had a ramified microglia arbor on the same day that division was complete (82%).
source: Original microglia often had extensive processes, which were maintained during the division and generation of new microglia (95%), and newly generated microglia frequently had a ramified microglia arbor on the same day that division was complete (82%).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of division events during high-frequency imaging.

claim: Cells generated from divisions persisted over time, moving away from one another to establish their own territories (100% of cells).
source: Cells generated from these divisions persisted over time, moving away from one another to establish their own territories (100% of cells; Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by tracking of newly divided cells shown in Figure 4.

claim: In some cases, cells divided twice, with the first division occurring rapidly, typically within 4 hr, and the cells migrating away from one another before adopting a doublet morphology and dividing again in less than 8 hr.
source: Notably, in some cases, we observed cells dividing twice (Figure 4C,D). The first division occurred rapidly, typically within 4 hr, and the cells migrated away from one another. These cells then adopted a doublet morphology and divided again in less than 8 hr (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is supported by high-frequency imaging data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: The rate of microglial division did not appear to be spatially regulated as microglia in close proximity divided at different times.
source: The rate of microglial division did not appear to be spatially regulated as microglia in close proximity divided at different times (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the spatial distribution of division events shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Microglial numbers roughly doubled over the 24-hr imaging period.
source: Microglial numbers roughly doubled over this imaging period in our animals (Figure 4E), and 3D nearest-neighbor numbers fell as microglia were generated (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of microglial numbers shown in Figure 4E.

claim: 3D nearest-neighbor numbers fell as microglia were generated during the 24-hr imaging period.
source: Microglial numbers roughly doubled over this imaging period in our animals (Figure 4E), and 3D nearest-neighbor numbers fell as microglia were generated (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by nearest neighbor analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Microglia translocation index during 4 hr intervals over 24 hr was ~8 μm.
source: To determine how mobile microglia were during the peak of repopulation, we tracked a small, identified subset of microglia in three of these animals. Microglia translocation index during 4 hr intervals over 24 hr was ~8 μm (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is supported by translocation analysis shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Most microglia did not move by more than 10–20 μm over the 24 hr during peak repopulation.
source: Overall, most microglia did not move by more than 10–20 μm over the 24 hr. The proportion of microglia that moved 20–30 μm was small during this time course (Figure 4J).
evidence: This is supported by translocation analysis shown in Figure 4J.

claim: Only 7% of microglia during the 24-hr peak repopulation period did not divide, and 5% adopted a doublet morphology that persisted throughout the imaging session.
source: More in-depth analysis of one of the animals to track and classify microglia showed that only 7% of microglia during this time did not divide, and 5% of these adopted a doublet morphology that persisted throughout the imaging session, suggesting they may divide at a later time.
evidence: This is supported by detailed tracking analysis in one animal.

claim: Of new cells during peak repopulation, 20% were born by rapid division, while only 2% of microglia were born of secondary divisions.
source: Of new cells, 20% were born by rapid division, while only 2% of microglia were born of secondary divisions in this mouse (Figure 4K).
evidence: This is supported by classification of division types shown in Figure 4K.

claim: The majority of the remaining microglia have a remarkable capacity to divide rapidly.
source: Overall, this points to a remarkable capacity of the majority of the remaining microglia to divide rapidly and suggests that this rapid division may explain the fast repopulation of the cortex after depletion.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the high-frequency imaging data.

claim: Rapid division may explain the fast repopulation of the cortex after depletion.
source: Overall, this points to a remarkable capacity of the majority of the remaining microglia to divide rapidly and suggests that this rapid division may explain the fast repopulation of the cortex after depletion.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the high-frequency imaging data.

claim: With 50% of cells available for division, it is reasonable to believe that the repopulation observed from days 2 to 3 came purely from local doublet cell division.
source: With 50% of cells available for division, it is reasonable to believe that the repopulation we observed from days 2 to 3 in our daily imaging experiments in 11 animals (Figure 2) came purely from local doublet cell division if 50% of cells are capable of division (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This is supported by mathematical modeling results shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: In half of the animals imaged, only 10% of cells would need to be capable of division to repopulate the visual cortex.
source: In fact, in half of the animals imaged, only 10% of cells would need to be capable of division to repopulate the visual cortex.
evidence: This is supported by mathematical modeling results.

claim: The local division of remaining microglia is likely responsible for rapid repopulation with newly born microglia capable of further division and without the need for the migration of newly generated microglia from a different site of generation.
source: This data suggests that the local division of remaining microglia is likely responsible for rapid repopulation with newly born microglia capable of further division and without the need for the migration of newly generated microglia from a different site of generation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the mathematical modeling results.

claim: At the peak of depletion (7 days of PLX), the remaining microglia exhibited a ramified morphology with extensive processes similar to the basal microglia process ramification under steady-state conditions.
source: At the peak of depletion (7 days of PLX), the remaining microglia exhibited a ramified morphology with extensive processes similar to the basal microglia process ramification under steady-state conditions (Figure 6B–C) and an increase in soma size that was not statistically significant (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis shown in Figure 6B-C,F.

claim: In the early phase of repopulation (day 1 – day 3), the newly born microglia appear ramified with secondary processes and have an enlarged soma.
source: In the early phase of repopulation (day 1 – day 3), the newly born microglia appear ramified with secondary processes (Figure 6B–E) and have an enlarged soma (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis shown in Figure 6B-E,F.

claim: There is an overshoot in the maximum number of intersections and the integrated area under the Sholl curve at 5 days of repopulation, which coincides with the increase in the number of microglia.
source: After this, a more complex arbor begins to form (Figure 6B–E), whereby there is an overshoot in the maximum number of intersections and the integrated area under the Sholl curve at 5 days of repopulation, which coincides with our increase in the number of microglia in our original repopulation data (Figures 2B and 5C).
evidence: This is supported by Sholl analysis shown in Figure 6B-E.

claim: Slight hyperramification is maintained for as long as 30 days of repopulation, despite a return to baseline numbers of microglia and a return to a smaller soma size.
source: This slight hyperramification is maintained for as long as we imaged (30 days of repopulation; Figure 6C–D), despite a return to baseline numbers of microglia (Figure 3B) and a return to a smaller soma size and full width half max quantification (Figure 6E–F).
evidence: This is supported by Sholl analysis and soma size measurements shown in Figure 6C-F.

claim: P2Y12-KO animals were hyporamified as compared to CX3CR1-GFP mice at baseline.
source: P2Y12-KO animals were hyporamified as compared to CX3CR1-GFP mice at baseline (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and did not show the hyperramification following repopulation as observed in the CX3CR1-GFP mice (Figure 6G–K; Figure 6—figure supplement 1), although similar changes in soma size were observed (Figure 6K).
evidence: This is supported by Sholl analysis comparing genotypes shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: P2Y12-KO animals did not show the hyperramification following repopulation as observed in the CX3CR1-GFP mice.
source: P2Y12-KO animals were hyporamified as compared to CX3CR1-GFP mice at baseline (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and did not show the hyperramification following repopulation as observed in the CX3CR1-GFP mice (Figure 6G–K; Figure 6—figure supplement 1), although similar changes in soma size were observed (Figure 6K).
evidence: This is supported by Sholl analysis comparing genotypes shown in Figure 6G-K.

claim: Newly born microglia rapidly acquire complex morphologies in a process that is independent of P2Y12.
source: Therefore, newly born microglia rapidly acquire complex morphologies in a process that is independent of P2Y12. However, newly born microglia exhibit a chronic hyperramification that distinguish them from microglia in control conditions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the morphological analysis comparing wild-type and P2Y12-KO mice.

claim: Newly born microglia exhibit a chronic hyperramification that distinguish them from microglia in control conditions.
source: Therefore, newly born microglia rapidly acquire complex morphologies in a process that is independent of P2Y12. However, newly born microglia exhibit a chronic hyperramification that distinguish them from microglia in control conditions.
evidence: This is supported by Sholl analysis showing persistent hyperramification.

claim: This hyperramification does not occur in the absence of P2Y12.
source: This hyperramification does not occur in the absence of P2Y12.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of morphology in wild-type and P2Y12-KO mice.

claim: PLX treatment led to only a modest decrease in motility.
source: PLX treatment led to only a modest decrease in motility (Figure 7D), as imaged over a 1-hr period, suggesting that the 20–30% of microglia that remain after depletion, not only have full arbors, but are motile and can effectively interact with elements in the parenchyma.
evidence: This is supported by motility analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The 20–30% of microglia that remain after depletion not only have full arbors, but are motile and can effectively interact with elements in the parenchyma.
source: PLX treatment led to only a modest decrease in motility (Figure 7D), as imaged over a 1-hr period, suggesting that the 20–30% of microglia that remain after depletion, not only have full arbors, but are motile and can effectively interact with elements in the parenchyma.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the motility data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: As new microglia were generated after depletion, microglial motility recovered such that the increase in movement correlated with the increase in the number of microglia over time.
source: As new microglia were generated after depletion, microglial motility recovered such that the increase in movement correlated with the increase in the number of microglia over time.
evidence: This is supported by motility analysis during repopulation.

claim: During the later stages of repopulation (day 21 day 30), there was no significant difference in basal microglia process motility and long-term stability as compared to baseline.
source: In addition, during the later stages of repopulation (day 21 day 30), we found no significant difference in basal microglia process motility and long-term stability as compared to baseline (Figure 7D–F).
evidence: This is supported by motility analysis shown in Figure 7D-F.

claim: Repopulation can be divided in two stages: early and late repopulation.
source: Combined with our previous data on microglia repopulation, these data suggest that repopulation can be divided in two stages: early and late repopulation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the morphology and motility data.

claim: As microglia mature in the later stages of repopulation (day 7 – day 30), they exhibit more complex arbors suggesting a dysregulation in their morphology.
source: As microglia mature in the later stages of repopulation (day 7 – day 30), they exhibit more complex arbors suggesting a dysregulation in their morphology.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Sholl analysis data.

claim: The long-term change in morphology does not impact microglial motility which resembles basal microglial states.
source: This long-term change in morphology, however, does not impact microglial motility which resembles basal microglial states (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the motility data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: During the early and late stages of repopulation, no changes in motility indices were observed in P2Y12-KO mice.
source: To complement the morphology assessment (Figure 6), we set out to determine the dynamics of newly born microglia in P2Y12-KO mice. Overall, during the early and late stages of repopulation, we did not observe any changes in motility indices in these mice (Figure 7G,H,I and Figure 7—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This is supported by motility analysis in P2Y12-KO mice shown in Figure 7G,H,I and supplementary figures.

claim: P2Y12 KO mice appeared to have lower motility in the early stages of repopulation (D1-D3), as well lower instability and stability indices than CX3CR1-GFP mice.
source: However, P2Y12 KO mice appeared to have lower motility in the early stages of repopulation (D1-D3), as well lower instability and stability indices than CX3CR1-GFP mice (Figure 7—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of motility indices shown in Figure 7—figure supplements 1–3.

claim: Following 7 days of PLX, the remaining microglia population survey a much smaller area than observed under basal conditions due to their reduced numbers.
source: Following 7 days of PLX, the remaining microglia population survey a much smaller area than observed under basal conditions due to their reduced numbers.
evidence: This is supported by surveillance analysis.

claim: Microglial surveillance recovers at day 3 of repopulation when microglial numbers return to baseline values and is maintained until day 30.
source: Microglial surveillance recovers at day 3 of repopulation when microglial numbers return to baseline values and is maintained until day 30 (Figure 7K).
evidence: This is supported by surveillance analysis shown in Figure 7K.

claim: When surveillance was normalized to the process coverage in the first time point to account for the loss of microglia with depletion, individual microglia surveilled their territory in the same manner throughout the control, depletion, and repopulation conditions.
source: When surveillance was normalized to the process coverage in the first time point (t=0mins) to account for the loss of microglia with depletion, we found that individual microglia surveilled their territory in the same manner throughout the control, depletion, and repopulation conditions (Figure 7L).
evidence: This is supported by normalized surveillance analysis shown in Figure 7L.

claim: The surveillance pattern was similar in the absence of P2Y12, although P2Y12-KO microglia appeared to be less efficient at surveilling the brain than CX3CR1-GFP microglia.
source: The surveillance pattern was similar in the absence of P2Y12, although P2Y12-KO microglia appeared to be less efficient at surveilling the brain than CX3CR1-GFP microglia (Figure 7—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by surveillance analysis in P2Y12-KO mice shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4.

claim: The difference in surveillance efficiency between P2Y12-KO and CX3CR1-GFP microglia is largely due to the less ramified arbor in P2Y12 KO microglia, as it was less apparent when surveillance was normalized to the first time point to account for morphology.
source: This difference is largely due to the less ramified arbor in P2Y12 KO microglia, as it was less apparent when surveillance was normalized to the first time point to account for morphology (Figure 7—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the normalized surveillance data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 5.

claim: P2Y12 KO microglia were more efficient at surveying the brain during PLX treatment.
source: Interestingly, it appeared that P2Y12 KO microglia were more efficient at surveying the brain during PLX treatment (Figure 7M–N; Figure 7—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by surveillance analysis shown in Figure 7M-N and Figure 7—figure supplement 5.

claim: Newly-born microglia mature within days of repopulation, acquire complex arbors, and survey the environment effectively.
source: Based on these findings, we conclude that newly-born microglia mature within days of repopulation, acquire complex arbors, and survey the environment effectively.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the morphology, motility, and surveillance data.

claim: While P2Y12 may mediate the microglial landscape under basal conditions, it likely plays a minor role in newly born microglia ontogeny and maturation.
source: Also, while P2Y12 may mediate the microglial landscape under basal conditions (Eyo et al., 2018), it likely plays a minor role in newly born microglia ontogeny and maturation (Figures 2, 6 and 7).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the comparison between wild-type and P2Y12-KO mice, supported by citation.

claim: Microglia at all stages of depletion and repopulation responded robustly to laser ablation injury.
source: Analysis of the average of all vectors moving towards the core showed that microglia at all stages of depletion and repopulation responded robustly to laser ablation injury (Figure 8F,G).
evidence: This is supported by laser ablation response analysis shown in Figure 8F,G.

claim: Both the maximum magnitude and the integrated response to laser ablation were similar across conditions.
source: Both the maximum magnitude and the integrated response (area under the curve) were similar across conditions (Figure 8G,H).
evidence: This is supported by laser ablation response analysis shown in Figure 8G,H.

claim: Under PLX treatment, the remaining microglia, although less motile, sparse, and randomly organized in the cortex, responded robustly to laser ablation injury with only a slight trend toward a decreased response.
source: It is interesting to note that, under PLX treatment, the remaining microglia, although less motile, sparse, and randomly organized in the cortex, responded robustly to laser ablation injury with only a slight trend toward a decreased response (Figure 8F,G,H).
evidence: This is supported by laser ablation response analysis shown in Figure 8F,G,H.

claim: There was no difference in the maximum convergence at 60 min and the area under the curve value at each time point during laser ablation response.
source: Similar to the directional velocity measure, there was no difference in the maximum convergence at 60 min and the area under the curve value at each time point (Figure 8J,K).
evidence: This is supported by convergence analysis shown in Figure 8J,K.

claim: The newly-born microglia during the early phases of repopulation can respond robustly to focal laser ablation injury.
source: This suggests that the newly-born microglia during the early phases of repopulation can respond robustly to focal laser ablation injury.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the laser ablation response data.

claim: Newly born microglia retain the necessary sensors such as P2Y12 and internal machinery to respond to injury.
source: This is an indication that microglia retain the necessary sensors such as P2Y12 and internal machinery to respond to injury.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the laser ablation response data.

claim: Microglia behave differently under anesthesia.
source: Because a growing body of literature suggests that microglia behave differently under anesthesia (Stowell et al., 2019a; Li et al., 2012; Sun et al., 2019), we wanted to capture the dynamics of microglia in the absence of anesthesia to avoid potentially inducing long-term alteration in microglial movement and turnover during repopulation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Microglia maintain their numbers and territories under basal conditions.
source: In this study, we characterized in detail the dynamics of adult microglia ontogeny and maturation in the visual cortex of mice. Because microglia behave differently in awake vs. anesthetized states (Stowell et al., 2019a; Sun et al., 2019; Liu, 2019), we used an awake in vivo chronic imaging setup to track microglial repopulation. First, we showed that microglia maintain their numbers and territories under basal conditions.
evidence: This is a summary of findings supported by in vivo imaging data and citations.

claim: Microglia can divide rapidly and continuously to repopulate the brain within a few days after partial depletion with the colony stimulating factor one receptor (CSF1R) inhibitor, PLX, in a manner that is largely independent of signaling through the P2Y12R.
source: Next, we found that microglia can divide rapidly and continuously to repopulate the brain within a few days after partial depletion with the colony stimulating factor one receptor (CSF1R) inhibitor, PLX, in a manner that is largely independent of signaling through the P2Y12R.
evidence: This is a summary of findings supported by in vivo imaging and comparison of wild-type and P2Y12-KO mice.

claim: A mathematical model based on the imaged kinetics of division confirmed that the repopulation was driven by very rapid, local self-renewal by surviving microglia.
source: A mathematical model based on the imaged kinetics of division confirmed that the repopulation was driven by very rapid, local self-renewal by surviving microglia, which transition to a doublet morphology, divide, and migrate apart before undergoing the next cycle of division.
evidence: This is a summary of findings supported by mathematical modeling.

claim: Surviving microglia transition to a doublet morphology, divide, and migrate apart before undergoing the next cycle of division.
source: A mathematical model based on the imaged kinetics of division confirmed that the repopulation was driven by very rapid, local self-renewal by surviving microglia, which transition to a doublet morphology, divide, and migrate apart before undergoing the next cycle of division.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo imaging data.

claim: Newly born microglia mature rapidly both structurally and functionally.
source: Finally, we found that newly born microglia mature rapidly both structurally and functionally and that P2Y12 modulates morphological changes following repopulation.
evidence: This is a summary of findings supported by morphological and functional analyses.

claim: P2Y12 modulates morphological changes following repopulation.
source: Finally, we found that newly born microglia mature rapidly both structurally and functionally and that P2Y12 modulates morphological changes following repopulation.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of morphology in wild-type and P2Y12-KO mice.

claim: Microglia are thought to be long-lived cells, self-renewing slowly and stochastically under unperturbed physiological conditions in the brain with an average lifetime of four years in the human cortex.
source: Microglia are thought to be long-lived cells, self-renewing slowly and stochastically under unperturbed physiological conditions in the brain with an average lifetime of four years in the human cortex (Réu et al., 2017), and 15 months in the mouse (Füger et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Microglia have an average lifetime of 15 months in the mouse.
source: Microglia are thought to be long-lived cells, self-renewing slowly and stochastically under unperturbed physiological conditions in the brain with an average lifetime of four years in the human cortex (Réu et al., 2017), and 15 months in the mouse (Füger et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Microglia can rapidly repopulate the brain when their niche has been depleted.
source: Despite their stability, microglia can rapidly repopulate the brain when their niche has been depleted (Bruttger et al., 2015; Elmore et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: During the height of repopulation, ~50% of cells adopted a doublet morphology indicative of an impending division.
source: We observed that during the height of repopulation, ~50% of cells adopted a doublet morphology indicative of an impending division, suggesting that most residual cells are capable of proliferating, and 95% of those cells divided in a 24-hr period.
evidence: This is supported by quantification of doublet cells during high-frequency imaging.

claim: Most residual cells are capable of proliferating, and 95% of those cells divided in a 24-hr period.
source: We observed that during the height of repopulation, ~50% of cells adopted a doublet morphology indicative of an impending division, suggesting that most residual cells are capable of proliferating, and 95% of those cells divided in a 24-hr period.
evidence: This is supported by tracking of doublet cells during high-frequency imaging.

claim: At the height of repopulation, division could occur very rapidly, with a cell adopting a doublet morphology and undergoing division within 4 hr.
source: In contrast, at the height of repopulation, division could occur very rapidly, with a cell adopting a doublet morphology and undergoing division within 4 hr.
evidence: This is supported by high-frequency imaging data.

claim: Rapidly dividing cells can undergo a secondary division within the 24-hr imaging period.
source: These rapidly dividing cells can undergo a secondary division within our 24-imaging period.
evidence: This is supported by high-frequency imaging data.

claim: This secondary division could occur in both cells generated from the first division, suggesting a remarkable capacity for proliferation in residual microglia.
source: This secondary division could occur in both cells generated from the first division, suggesting a remarkable capacity for proliferation in residual microglia.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the high-frequency imaging data.

claim: Microglia are morphologically and transcriptionally diverse, with high-throughput single-cell transcriptomics identifying distinct subpopulations of microglia with unique molecular signatures that change with age and in response to insults.
source: While we cannot discern whether these differences in division rates are tied to specific subpopulations of microglia, it is well known that microglia are morphologically and transcriptionally diverse, with high-throughput single-cell transcriptomics identifying distinct subpopulations of microglia with unique molecular signatures that change with age and in response to insults (Hammond et al., 2019; Ayata et al., 2018; Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Microglial heterogeneity is also seen across various brain regions.
source: This heterogeneity in microglia is also seen across various brain regions (Hammond et al., 2019; Ayata et al., 2018; O'Koren et al., 2019; De Biase et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: It has been suggested that the remaining microglia after depletion are a specialized CSF1R-inhibitor resistant population of Galectin-3-progenitor-like microglia.
source: For instance, it has been suggested that the remaining microglia after depletion are a specialized CSF1R-inhibitor resistant population of Galectin-3-progenitor-like microglia (Zhan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Proliferating cells can be Galectin-3 positive or negative.
source: We did not see a correspondence between our doublet morphologies and Galectin-3 expression, which supports the idea that proliferating cells can be Galectin-3 positive or negative (Zhan et al., 2020), although other factors could define proliferating microglial populations.
evidence: This is supported by Galectin-3 immunostaining data and citation to previous research.

claim: In the retina, microglia repopulate from a distinct source and migrate through the optic nerve to repopulate the rest of the retina.
source: A similar scenario has been observed in the retina where microglia repopulate from a distinct source and migrate through the optic nerve to repopulate the rest of the retina (Huang et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Newly born microglia acquire mature characteristics such as baseline motility, surveillance, and response to acute laser ablation remarkably quickly.
source: We show that newly born microglia acquire mature characteristics such as baseline motility, surveillance, and response to acute laser ablation remarkably quickly.
evidence: This is a summary of findings supported by motility, surveillance, and laser ablation data.

claim: Dividing doublet microglia have an extensive, motile arbor which is maintained through the division such that the two resulting cells already have extensive processes which surveil the environment and can respond to injury.
source: In fact, dividing doublet microglia have an extensive, motile arbor which is maintained through the division such that the two resulting cells already have extensive processes which surveil the environment and can respond to injury.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo imaging data.

claim: Microglial expression in newly repopulated microglia recapitulates some aspects of neonatal microglia expression patterns.
source: While microglial expression in newly repopulated microglia recapitulates some aspects of neonatal microglia expression patterns (Zhan et al., 2019; Zhan et al., 2020), we did not observe the typical morphologies of microglia or changes in process dynamics and responses to injury that could indicate a less mature phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Developing microglia transition from an ameboid morphology to a ramified morphology at around post-natal day 30.
source: Developing microglia transition from an ameboid morphology to a ramified morphology at around post-natal day 30 (Orłowski et al., 2003), and while microglial dynamics have not been extensively studied in development, early life microglia have few processes and are migratory (Kierdorf et al., 2013; Hoeffel et al., 2015; Ginhoux et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Early life microglia have few processes and are migratory.
source: Developing microglia transition from an ameboid morphology to a ramified morphology at around post-natal day 30 (Orłowski et al., 2003), and while microglial dynamics have not been extensively studied in development, early life microglia have few processes and are migratory (Kierdorf et al., 2013; Hoeffel et al., 2015; Ginhoux et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Newly born microglia did not exhibit ameboid morphologies, and somas tended to not move more than 10–20 µm.
source: Since newly born microglia did not exhibit ameboid morphologies, and somas tended to not move more than 10–20 µm, this suggests that if microglia do revert to a developmental program when they are first generated in the adult brain, this program does not significantly alter their physiological functions.
evidence: This is supported by morphological and translocation data.

claim: If microglia do revert to a developmental program when they are first generated in the adult brain, this program does not significantly alter their physiological functions.
source: Since newly born microglia did not exhibit ameboid morphologies, and somas tended to not move more than 10–20 µm, this suggests that if microglia do revert to a developmental program when they are first generated in the adult brain, this program does not significantly alter their physiological functions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the morphological and functional data.

claim: Newly born microglia may go through an accelerated maturation program, as expression also matures much faster than the stepwise development of microglia over a period of weeks in early life.
source: Alternately, they may go through an accelerated maturation program, as expression also matures much faster than the stepwise development of microglia over a period of weeks in early life (Zhan et al., 2019; Bennett et al., 2016; Matcovitch-Natan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to previous research.

claim: After 30 days of repopulation, new microglia largely adopt the gene expression profile of control microglia.
source: While many studies have shown that after 30 days of repopulation, new microglia largely adopt the gene expression profile of control microglia (Elmore et al., 2015; Zhan et al., 2019), several observations in our study suggest that adult born microglia may not be identical to their yolk-sac-generated counterparts.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Adult born microglia may not be identical to their yolk-sac-generated counterparts.
source: While many studies have shown that after 30 days of repopulation, new microglia largely adopt the gene expression profile of control microglia (Elmore et al., 2015; Zhan et al., 2019), several observations in our study suggest that adult born microglia may not be identical to their yolk-sac-generated counterparts.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the morphological data showing persistent hyperramification.

claim: After repopulation, microglia morphology changed with a hyper-ramification of the processes and more microglia adopted a doublet-like morphology with an elongated cell body.
source: We found that after repopulation, microglia morphology changed with a hyper-ramification of the processes and that more microglia adopted a doublet-like morphology with an elongated cell body.
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis.

claim: These morphological changes persisted for a month after the cessation of PLX, suggesting that newly born microglia may take on a unique phenotype that persists long after microglia are mature.
source: As these changes persisted for a month after the cessation of PLX, it may be that newly born microglia take on a unique phenotype that persists long after microglia are mature.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the morphological data.

claim: Hyper-ramification of microglia is typically associated with periods of enhanced plasticity such as that following monocular deprivation in the developing visual cortex.
source: Hyper-ramification of microglia is typically associated with periods of enhanced plasticity such as that following monocular deprivation in the developing visual cortex (Huang et al., 2018b) and with chronically stressed animals in a model of posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) (Smith et al., 2019) where microglia transition from their normal ramified morphology to a hyper-ramified state, characterized by an increase in primary and secondary processes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Hyper-ramification of microglia is associated with chronically stressed animals in a model of posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD).
source: Hyper-ramification of microglia is typically associated with periods of enhanced plasticity such as that following monocular deprivation in the developing visual cortex (Huang et al., 2018b) and with chronically stressed animals in a model of posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) (Smith et al., 2019) where microglia transition from their normal ramified morphology to a hyper-ramified state, characterized by an increase in primary and secondary processes.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: A similar microglial response, which has been referred to as arrested hyper-ramification, is observed during aging and in response to specific neurotoxins.
source: A similar microglial response, which has been referred to as arrested hyper-ramification, is also observed during aging and in response to specific neurotoxins (Streit et al., 1999; Streit et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The presence of a persistently increased number of microglia with elongated, doublet-like cell bodies after repopulation could be indicative of further morphological alteration of newly born microglia.
source: The presence of a persistently increased number of microglia with elongated, doublet-like cell bodies, after repopulation, could be indicative of further morphological alteration of newly born microglia, but it could also suggest an increased capacity for division as similar doublets have been identified as a source of dividing cells in another study (Füger et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The persistently increased number of microglia with elongated, doublet-like cell bodies could suggest an increased capacity for division as similar doublets have been identified as a source of dividing cells in another study.
source: The presence of a persistently increased number of microglia with elongated, doublet-like cell bodies, after repopulation, could be indicative of further morphological alteration of newly born microglia, but it could also suggest an increased capacity for division as similar doublets have been identified as a source of dividing cells in another study (Füger et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citation to previous research.

claim: If Galectin-3+ microglia that remain after depletion have increased capacity for division, they may divide to produce new microglia that are distinct from yolk sac-generated microglia and rapidly take on mature characteristics.
source: If Galectin-3+ microglia that remain after depletion Zhan et al., 2020 have increased capacity for division, they may divide to produce new microglia that are distinct from yolk sac-generated microglia and rapidly take on mature characteristics, contributing to a different phenotype of adult vs. yolk-sac born microglia.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on citation to previous research.

claim: The Galectin-3+ cells may remain in the population as persistent doublet cells primed for division and self-renewal.
source: The Galectin-3+ cells may remain in the population as persistent doublet cells primed for division and self-renewal.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation.

claim: While adult born microglia appear to rapidly take on their mature roles in the brain, their characteristics may differ in subtle ways from microglia that are generated in the yolk sac and populate the brain in development.
source: Thus, while adult born microglia appear to rapidly take on their mature roles in the brain, their characteristics may differ in subtle ways from microglia that are generated in the yolk sac and populate the brain in development.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the findings.

claim: Efficient rejuvenation of old 'senescent' microglia in the diseased brain with new microglia through depletion and repopulation can generate a new population of microglia with improved functions.
source: It is possible that efficient rejuvenation of old 'senescent' microglia in the diseased brain with new microglia through depletion and repopulation can generate a new population of microglia with improved functions (Rice et al., 2015; Spangenberg et al., 2016; Elmore et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: It remains unclear whether the chronologically younger newly born cell is also biologically younger.
source: However, it is important to recognize that it remains unclear whether the chronologically younger newly born cell is also biologically younger.
evidence: This is a statement of uncertainty about the biological age of newly born microglia.

claim: It is not known whether the division of microglia is symmetrical or asymmetrical.
source: In fact, we do not yet understand the biological process of microglia repopulation, and it is not known whether the division of microglia is symmetrical or asymmetrical.
evidence: This is a statement of uncertainty about the mechanism of microglial division.

claim: Newly born microglia may go through a stepwise expression program that partly recapitulates development, giving them younger functional characteristics.
source: Newly born microglia may go through a stepwise expression program that partly recapitulates development, giving them younger functional characteristics, or they may acquire all the epigenetic and cytoplasmic features of their 'aged' parent cell, leading to repopulation but not 'rejuvenation' of the microglia niche (Zhan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Newly born microglia may acquire all the epigenetic and cytoplasmic features of their 'aged' parent cell, leading to repopulation but not 'rejuvenation' of the microglia niche.
source: Newly born microglia may go through a stepwise expression program that partly recapitulates development, giving them younger functional characteristics, or they may acquire all the epigenetic and cytoplasmic features of their 'aged' parent cell, leading to repopulation but not 'rejuvenation' of the microglia niche (Zhan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citation to previous research.

claim: If newly-born cells acquire all the epigenetic and cytoplasmic features of their 'aged' parent cell, this could explain why the newly-born cells acquire mature characteristics and functions early in the repopulation phase.
source: This latter option could also explain why the newly-born cells acquire mature characteristics and functions early in the repopulation phase.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation.

claim: A combination of exogenous and endogenous signaling mechanisms may contribute to microglia rapid repopulation and spatial organization.
source: A combination of exogenous and endogenous signaling mechanisms may contribute to microglia rapid repopulation and spatial organization.
evidence: This is a general statement about potential mechanisms.

claim: Colony stimulating factor 1 (CSF-1) and interleukin one receptor (IL1R) regulate microglia proliferation.
source: Recent evidence has shed light onto some of the extracellular signals that shape repopulation, including those that regulate microglia proliferation such as colony stimulating factor 1 (CSF-1) and interleukin one receptor (IL1R), and those that regulate migration such as fractalkine through its receptor, CX3CR1 (10, 11, 20).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Fractalkine through its receptor, CX3CR1, regulates microglial migration.
source: Recent evidence has shed light onto some of the extracellular signals that shape repopulation, including those that regulate microglia proliferation such as colony stimulating factor 1 (CSF-1) and interleukin one receptor (IL1R), and those that regulate migration such as fractalkine through its receptor, CX3CR1 (10, 11, 20).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: NF-ΚB signaling has been shown to be important for microglia to repopulate fully.
source: A gradient or threshold of these factors may start intracellular cascades in microglia that trigger division and migration, such as NF-ΚB signaling, which has been shown to be important for microglia to repopulate fully (Zhan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The P2Y12 receptor does not modulate newly born microglial maturation despite effects of P2Y12 loss on microglia ramification.
source: In addition, we show that the P2Y12 receptor does not modulate newly born microglial maturation (Figures 6 and 7F) despite effects of P2Y12 loss on microglia ramification (Figure 6—figure supplement 1; Haynes et al., 2006; Sipe et al., 2016), and it does not affect doublet formation, repopulation, or the acquisition of microglial territories (as reflected by changes in nearest neighbor quantification) in the visual cortex (Figures 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of wild-type and P2Y12-KO mice and citations to previous research.

claim: P2Y12 does not affect doublet formation, repopulation, or the acquisition of microglial territories in the visual cortex.
source: In addition, we show that the P2Y12 receptor does not modulate newly born microglial maturation (Figures 6 and 7F) despite effects of P2Y12 loss on microglia ramification (Figure 6—figure supplement 1; Haynes et al., 2006; Sipe et al., 2016), and it does not affect doublet formation, repopulation, or the acquisition of microglial territories (as reflected by changes in nearest neighbor quantification) in the visual cortex (Figures 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of wild-type and P2Y12-KO mice.

claim: Microglia repopulate and mature in a P2Y12-independent manner.
source: All together, this suggest that microglia repopulate and mature in a P2Y12-independent manner.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the comparison between wild-type and P2Y12-KO mice.

claim: The progressive distribution of microglia to achieve tiling during repopulation is most likely maintained by lateral inhibition mechanisms and homeostatic microglia-specific genes such as Sal1 and Mafb.
source: The progressive distribution of microglia to achieve tiling during repopulation is most likely maintained by lateral inhibition mechanisms and homeostatic microglia-specific genes such as Sal1 and Mafb—which both maintain microglia in a ramified nonclustered state (Matcovitch-Natan et al., 2016; Buttgereit et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Because microglial numbers overshoot their target during the early stages of repopulation, it is likely that astrocytes may be recruited to phagocytose excess newly-born microglia.
source: Because microglial numbers overshoot their target during the early stages of repopulation, it is also likely that astrocytes may be recruited to phagocytose excess newly-born microglia, and these cells may contribute to the extracellular environment that promotes microglial migration and maturation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation.

claim: Astrocytes may contribute to the extracellular environment that promotes microglial migration and maturation.
source: Because microglial numbers overshoot their target during the early stages of repopulation, it is also likely that astrocytes may be recruited to phagocytose excess newly-born microglia, and these cells may contribute to the extracellular environment that promotes microglial migration and maturation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation.

claim: An interplay of diverse factors likely contributes to microglia homeostasis following depletion, which may include endogenous mechanisms at play in specific populations of microglia, including Galectin-3+ cells, as well as exogenous factors that come from microglia, neurons, and astrocytes.
source: Altogether, an interplay of diverse factors likely contributes to microglia homeostasis following depletion, which may include endogenous mechanisms at play in specific populations of microglia, including Galectin-3+ cells, as well as exogenous factors that come from microglia, neurons, and astrocytes and work together to re-establish microglia numbers in the adult brain.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of potential mechanisms.

claim: Rejuvenation of adult microglia is driven by stochastic doublet cell division locally during repopulation, with newly born cells rapidly able to take on their roles in the brain.
source: Together our results build on current adult microglia ontogeny research showing that rejuvenation of adult microglia is driven by stochastic doublet cell division locally during repopulation, with newly born cells rapidly able to take on their roles in the brain.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: Loss of P2Y12 impacts microglial morphologies during repopulation but seems to play a minor role in microglial division.
source: Loss of P2Y12 impacts microglial morphologies during repopulation but seems to play a minor role in microglial division.
evidence: This is a summary of findings comparing wild-type and P2Y12-KO mice.

claim: Mathematical modeling supports the idea that division of residual microglia alone can fill the microglia niche following depletion.
source: In addition, our mathematical modeling supports the idea that division of residual microglia alone can fill the microglia niche following depletion.
evidence: This is a summary of the mathematical modeling results.
